utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We're again without Judge Chowhan, who is still unwell; but as yesterday, we have decided to continue in his absence. I note also that Mr. Pavkovic is not here today, but I understand, Mr. Aleksic, he's content that the proceedings continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. During the course of the day our client is going to give his approval for the proceedings to continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are a couple of administrative matters I would like to deal with. We are receiving a regular flow of applications to finally admit documents following translation, two of these from the Prosecution relate to P1975 and P3074. Can Defence counsel indicate if there is any submission to be made in relation to either of these? Now, if that cannot be answered immediately, could we have an answer, please, after the first break. The second matter I wish to raise is, Mr. Lukic, with you. The Prosecution asked for information to help them identify the personnel who are on your 65 ter list as numbers 44 to 49, these are PJP commanders. The Chamber e-mailed your legal assistant on the 13th and asked for an immediate response whether you had complied with the request to provide detail on the father's name for these witnesses. Regrettably, we have had no reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I was informed just now, regrettably, we haven't received those data from the Government of Serbia yet, but we'll check it during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a not infrequent occurrence in relation to communications with your legal support staff that we do not get an answer as requested. So I would be grateful if you would try to encourage them to respond. We would not need to take up time in court if we had an explanation of the difficulties you are encountering. We appreciate there are difficulties in various circumstances here, but the fact that there are difficulties is not an excuse for not responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other matter I want to deal with also is for your attention and it is to do with the question of translation which you raised yesterday and I said I would inquire into. The words you used yesterday were: "I was just informed that all our documents are now rejected by the CLSS except for the witness statements." Now, I suspect that that statement is inaccurate in more than one respect. It suggests, first of all, that you had just received notification of rejection of documents. Do you know the date on which CLSS last rejected documents to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'm not dealing with the matter, and yesterday Mr. Ivetic told me something and I misrepresented to Your Honours. The problem is that the documents are rejected when we asked them to translate statements, witness statements. So whenever we ask for witness statements, we have to take some documents from the bundle, the same amount of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two basic points to be made first of all, Mr. Lukic. Rejection is a part of the process, a necessary part of the process, so that you can make use, continued use, of the exceptional facility that's been granted to your Defence alone to have another translator of your own do work for you; and that work can only be done on documents that are rejected, it's part of the process. The other general point that has to be made to you is this, that your Defence team seem intent on confrontation instead of compromise by negotiation. And every time something of this nature happens, instead of addressing it and trying to discuss a solution, the only way we ever get a solution is if I, other Judges, or some of the legal support staff become involved with CLSS. Now, my information is that that rejection took place on the 1st of February, which is almost three weeks ago, and that an e-mail was sent explaining the position and that there has been no contact since. Now, if that's true, it is ridiculous, because with a simple phone call yesterday, I've been able, I hope, to persuade CLSS to take the 40 documents that were rejected and try to deal with them, try their best, because they're already ahead of the 200 that they're supposed to do for you for February, they're already ahead of the game, they're into the March documents, as I understand the position. So with persuasion we can reach a situation where more will be done than perhaps was indicated at the beginning of the month. Three weeks is a long time in a trial like this. That rejection also occurred because of the production of statements for translation, as you've pointed out a little time ago. If you're doing your statements at this stage, then you are yourselves creating this problem because it will all have to be translated. And if there's going to be a lot of these statements, then you're going to have to find an imaginative way of dealing with the issues the, difficulties of translation that are going to arise dealing with these matters at this stage in the game, almost three years since your client first appeared here. So, Mr. Lukic, we would welcome a more cooperative approach from you towards translation and a recognition of the exceptional lengths to which the Trial Chamber and CLSS have gone so far and continue to go to try to resolve the translation problems that seem to bedevil your particular case. But there will come a time, and it may not be far away, when documents are going to be rejected because they have not been translated and the circumstances indicate that they should have been. We'll deal with that situation as and when we come to it. So far, as you know, we have tried to accommodate you throughout and we have, I would suggest, a very moderate stance taken by the Prosecution to enable this to be the position to try to ensure that the whole case you seek to present is presented. Now, these are the things I wanted to say about this and the immediate consequence of what I've just said is that you should, with a bit of humility, have further discussions with CLSS about the pages that were recently rejected to see if all of them or even some of them can be accommodated within their schedule. Now, just give me one moment before we proceed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll now continue with the evidence. Could you bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gavranic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry we've delayed the recommencement of your evidence slightly this morning. We had certain administrative matters to attend to, but we can now proceed with the evidence and your examination by Mr. Lukic will now continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning once again, Mr. Gavranic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Policemen of the SUP of Gnjilane and the relevant OUPs, did they tour the villages around the town of Gnjilane every day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of their ability at the time we really made an effort to patrol as many settlements as possible because this instilled confidence in the citizens in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm going to leave this area, but before doing that I'm going to put a few more questions in relation to that. Sometimes our technical stuff simply doesn't work. It's on my computer and I don't seem to be able to call it up, so -- very well. Now we can actually deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 6D614, page 342, paragraph 933.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think you have it there in hard copy, so you'll have to follow it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work did you make a distinction in terms of whether the injured party was a Serb or an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When testifying yesterday I already said, and I'll repeat it today again, it really didn't matter who it was and what their ethnic background was. It didn't even matter what their social status was in general. We dealt with all cases. We acted in relation to all the offences committed on the basis of what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at this paragraph, 933, and could you tell us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is the village of Zegra, Gnjilane, the 12th of April, 1999, aggravated theft under Article 166 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. According to a report by the injured party, namely, Jasari Rifat of the village of Zegra, an aggravated theft under Article 166 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia was committed on the 12th of April, 1999, and various kinds of electrical goods were appropriated. A criminal complaint KU 227/99 was filed against an unknown perpetrator and it was submitted to the municipal public prosecutor's office in Gnjilane. The offence was cleared up. It was committed by Pavic Stojadin, a civilian of the village of Zegra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Gavranic, one of the problems that we have is when something's being read, the person reading it tends to speak more quickly than normal. So when you're reading could you bear that in mind. And it's also important, because of the fact that you're both speaking the same language, to pause at the end of the question before you answer so that the translation can be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you tell us just briefly now, we see here that at the moment the crime was reported the perpetrator was unknown. Isn't that right? Isn't that evident?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was not a rare occurrence. When we would learn of a crime we would carry out an on-site investigation. We would see that it's an unknown perpetrator and then we would try to collect information, and on the basis of this information after a certain period of time we managed to unravel the case. This was precisely the case on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it sometimes happen that the perpetrator would remain unknown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that happens even in peacetime, let alone in wartime, yes, it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court page 20, paragraph 22, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us briefly again what took place there. You don't have to read this out loud. Just tell us about this Kabas murder.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the village of Kabas, Vitina municipality, 5th of May, 1999, a body of Mustafa Sefcet was found, born in 1947 in Vitina. The procedure was as I described. Through operative work we learned that the murder had been committed by Stoiljkovic Drago, known as Mozak, member of the Army of Yugoslavia. The security organ of the Army of Yugoslavia was informed about the event as well as the relevant officers within the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when you turn over a person to the security organs in the army, what further jurisdiction do you have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our jurisdiction ends there. Should we learn something else subsequently, then we provide it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like to move on to a different topic which has to do with the mass departure of civilians from your area. In which direction did civilians mostly go from your area in the beginning of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, in the early days of the bombing a large column of civilians left their area, first from Gnjilane and some surrounding villages and departed in the area of Vranje. However, in second waves, as we used to refer to them, when there was additional mass departure from the area covered by the Gnjilane SUP, these civilians were travelling in other directions as well, they went in the direction of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now -- we will later move on to details, but tell me this: Did you try to convince civilians to go back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. That was our standing task, if I may put it that way, because we had to talk to people and encourage them. The reasons were always the same. They were afraid of bombing because the bombing was incessant. The town of Gnjilane was bombed constantly, and also whenever residents of some villages noticed that the army was moving in the vicinity of their village, then they would leave their village because they knew that the army was the most frequent target. There were a lot of situations when the residents would come back, basically listening to our advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to details. Let me just first show you a document, 5D1100. You have the document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake. We need item 4. You can see it on the screen. This is the document of the command of the 52nd Motorised Brigade -- rather, Mixed Artillery Brigade, 7th of April, 1999. In item 4 it says: "Assist the MUP forces in the return and protection of displaced persons."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it happen in reality that the Army of Yugoslavia was assisting you in the return of citizens and was this military unit in your area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see item 4, and I see that this document was signed by Colonel Ratko Milinovic, who I have already mentioned. And out of all officers, and there were a number of them in the territory of Gnjilane SUP who were commanders of various military units, the best cooperation I had was precisely with him. This information is correct. He was the garrison commander in Gnjilane as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to put a question to you regarding the 6th of April, 1999, when the columns of civilians set out from, or rather, you tell us, do you remember from which villages these columns set out on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of April there were developments in the territory of our SUP where there were large movements of civilians and people leaving their homes. I remember the 6th of April because of the village of Prilepnica, which was quite a peculiar case in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were people leaving the area from Lovace and other areas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I were to elaborate on this, I would tell you that during this period of time the bombing was also intense and a number of villages were on the move, Lovace, Natovci, Donja Limoc [phoen], Crevnica. I remember that there was a fire covering 5 hectares in the vicinity of the village of Crevnica and it engulfed the entire village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you determine what caused this fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bombing, the bombing did, the forest was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the people who had left villages in columns on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you something about the Prilepnica case because it was quite specific and it marked a period in our lives at the time. Yes, I remember that on the 6th of April that village was on the move completely. I also remember that a delegation came looking for officers in our SUP, and this delegation was led by their priest, by imam, and they talked to the chief of police, Dragan Rizanovic. I had the occasion to see the words of imam who mentioned Dragan Peric Svetozar who was chief of crime police department heading the operations group that I had established to shed light on the most difficult crimes. Rizanovic was chief of police department, and these people asked for assistance not to move out because allegedly the Army of Yugoslavia had told them to move out. Since we could not affect this process we told them we would talk to them to see what this was all about and these people went back. I know that I attempted to find out from the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia about what was going on in that village. That's a small village away from Gnjilane, it's on a side road and it's surrounded by mountains and forests, and they came to this intersection which is popularly known as the intersection by the well. And talking to the officers and Colonel Milinovic who I had found via courier, I wasn't able to establish that anybody had told these residents to move out. They were already on the move, moving in the direction of Vranje, and we sent out a patrol to talk to them to tell them that this was not true, that this was misinformation. This patrol was from Kamenica and it covered that area. It was a traffic patrol. They talked to these people and these people came back. We did not have any information indicating that anybody who we had managed to contact in the Army of Yugoslavia had ordered them or told them anything of that nature. So these people came back. We gave them a guarantee, telling them that everything was all right, that they should not fall prey to various propaganda, misinformation, and people putting on false uniforms. And in return we promised them that a patrol, they call it a check-point, but it wasn't a check-point; it was a patrol. It was dangerous to have check-points due to NATO bombing. But we sent out a patrol and it was there in -- on that intersection for the following week during an entire -- during the entire time, it was near the village of Prilepnica. However, these people were on the move again a week later, and this is when the bombing was the gravest. As far as I remember, that was the most intense bombing on the 13th of April. And towards Macedonian border, towards Presevo and in the broader sector of the village of Kmetovac, which is not far from Prilepnica. The army positions there were bombed. It was first the residents of the area of Mucibaba who set out, that was the territory of Malisevo, Crna Cesme, and so on. And then the residents of Prilepnica joined them and they created a huge column on that road. The residents of Prilepnica once again got in touch with members of the police and the same person who had talked to them on the first occasion talked to them again. Rizanovic Dragan, chief of police department. However, this time nobody could convince them because this time this was a huge column comprising several villages. They were determined to go to Macedonia and the only thing they begged us for was to give them a patrol so that nobody would mistreat them on their way, stop them and so on, and in order to ensure this cooperation, because the imam knew a lot of people from the SUP, we gave them a traffic patrol and on that road leading to Kacanik this patrol escorted them. That was on the 13th and 14th of April, as I had told you. This large group of civilians was on the move on the 13th. This patrol did not come back for a long, long time and I was afraid that something had happened to them. I didn't know who was in that column, I didn't know what was happening during that time; however, when they came back they told us that pursuant to the request of imam they had escorted the column all the way. So this is what I know. This is somewhat atypical for Zegra, and Prilepnica, I remember these events well because they were unusual. As for additional problems of this nature, I did not have any other such problems in the territory of SUP Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, why initially would apparent refugees head in the direction of Vranje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They headed in the direction of Vranje because in Presevo and in Bujanovac I suppose there's a lot of Albanian residents, that's in the south of Serbia. So I assume that they went there because of them. They were travelling to the southern part of Serbia. Bujanovac is a town where there's -- where there is more Albanians than Serbs residing. This is the territory of the Vranje SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a clarification, you gave us this account in detail, but tell us this: How many people there were in that column, if you know, how many people were in the patrol and where did the patrol move, in what area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you, this was a large column of several thousand people. As I told you, several villages, not only residents of Prilepnica but other villages as well because the residents of Prilepnica just joined the column comprising residents of Malisevo, Crna Cesme and so on. My conclusion at the time was that they got scared by the bombing that night and some other reasons that I mentioned in the beginning of my testimony. So that was a column of several thousand people. As for the traffic patrol, and I allowed the chief of traffic to designate a patrol, they went ahead of them, ahead of the column, so as to make it clear. They were traffic policemen with white bands on their sleeves. And when people see that police was there, then nobody usually attacked or mistreated people. The only danger was that members of the KLA would frequently join the column, and this is why there was a risk. That is precisely what I was afraid of when the traffic patrol did not come back for a long time, I was worried that something had happened to them because of that. And if I may add this, on that occasion we were unable to establish, on the 14th, I talked to the members of the army but we were unable to establish who had set the residents of Prilepnica on the move again. We talked to these people near the intersection where they were. We didn't know who told them to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, was there just one patrol?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was just the patrol at the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one patrol but a reinforced one. We didn't dare just send two people. I think there were three or four policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see in e-court P1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: May I ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In terms of the police control that would have escorted and followed this column, are you able to tell me how the police would have been placed in terms of how they escorted this column? Would they have been interspersed along the way or would they have been within one block? Are you able to say how it would have been done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how this was translated to you, but there was just one patrol travelling in a patrol vehicle. They travelled ahead of the column. There were no other policemen, either along the road or anywhere else in the column. There was just one patrol at the head of the column in a patrol vehicle. There were a total of three or four policemen, because typically a patrol has two policemen and in this instance there were three or four of them because we were worried about their safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I wanted to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have this exhibit before you in the binder?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are minutes from the meeting held at the MUP staff on the 7th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 7, please, in B/C/S, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I did attend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you report about? What was your report about that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of several collegium meetings held in the course of the war in Pristina where we had the task of providing information on all security-related events taking place in the period between two collegium meetings. Here I also reported on the number of days when NATO had bombed our area. I reported that 184 crimes had been committed or 174.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on page 8 of these minutes, 168 crimes were general crimes, 16 were economic crimes. Criminal reports were submitted for 189 persons and 114 persons were arrested, taken into custody. I reported that public law and order was stable, that there had only been ten misdemeanours, which is not much. I also reported that I had arrested the deputy municipal public prosecutor and the chief of the market inspection for Gnjilane municipality, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were just checking something in the transcript, but for the most part it's in order. So after the beginning of the air-strikes, did you continue carrying out regular police work, police duties?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best we could in the given conditions. All regular work continued, but the stress was on throwing light on the most serious crimes. These were very different. There were murders, there was looting, burning, break-ins, robberies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time were there some new regulations in force, according to which the police acted?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We already established that in my testimony of yesterday, and these were the decrees that arrived in early April when war broke out. In addition to the decrees, we've already mentioned there was the decree on personal identity cards where the age limit was now 14 rather than 16. Previously a person had to be 16 to get a personal identity card. According to the new decree, a 14-year-old could get an identity card. There were other additional regulations, new regulations, governing the field of our work. There was also a decree which was important in our view, and that was the decree concerning the Law on Criminal Procedure, where powers were given to the police also in addition to the public prosecutor and the investigating judge in exceptional and urgent cases. In such cases, the police could carry out investigations and hand down detention, custody. This period was now prolonged. Previously the police could hold a person up to three days. With the new decree this was extended to 30 days. Also, keeping people in custody under the old regulations was 24 hours, but under this new decree a person could be held for longer than 24 hours but then the person would have to be handed over to the investigating judge at the first possible moment, as soon as the wartime conditions permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, do you know why there was a change in the age limit for identity cards at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why. It was a whole new system of regulations amending the existing regulations and legislation. There were a number of decrees issued in the wartime situation making more stringent all the measures that had been in place before and things were regulated slightly different than -- differently than they had been in peacetime, but I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have a witness, Dujkovic, who should be able to explain this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 -- Exhibit 6D614, page 972 -- paragraph 972.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something different on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, it's 6D614, that's the exhibit, page 348, item 972. I see that I have made a mistake, so now we'll move to page 398, item 1278. [In English] One point on the top, 1278.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who this person was, Slavko Simic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Mogila, Vitina municipality -- no, I remember some other last names from Zegra of civilians from Prilepnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this SPS deputy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the SPS deputy in Gnjilane municipality, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there other deputies there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another one. If you were to jog my memory, I'd remember him. There were two deputies among the persons we took into custody and the Gnjilane court said they were to be held in detention. There were two deputies from Gnjilane municipality and one of them was the one we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was Zoran Disic the other, was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember now. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, on the screen you see 1282?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was serious theft on the 25th of May, aggravated theft, that is, and it was Sebastijan Ademi, a civilian from Kmetovac who perpetrated this aggravated theft and he was remanded in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you arrest any other persons in Gnjilane who were in positions of power, of authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that I remember if you consider people in the economic sphere to have authority, there were people from state-owned companies in Gnjilane and Kosovska Kamenica. We didn't really pay attention in that situation to who was in what position and who held what office, whether he was a civil servant or a leader in society. So there was a very varied list if one looks at it statistically of persons who behaved inappropriately during the war and committed crimes. We treated them the same as any other citizens. They were all the same in my view, all equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court 6D334.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this about, what kind of document is this or collection of documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a case concerning the exhumation of some bodies. We received information, or rather, the policemen in the sector received information that in Vitina municipality there were six freshly dug graves. Acting on that information, we established, or rather, Zulfensa Diki [phoen] from Vitina municipality reported to the patrol that in the village of Donja Stubla in Vitina he had buried six of his relatives. We found those six relatives, or rather, we found those six grave mounds and we reported this to Zivorad Stankovic, the investigating judge, but because it was so dangerous the exhumation was carried out only a few days later. And it was established after the exhumation what the identity of the persons who were killed was. They were all Albanians, five from the village of Djilekare [phoen] and one from the village of Gornja Bulija [phoen]. It was established after the exhumation that all these persons had been killed from fire-arms, and according to the statement of Zulfensa Diki, all of them were killed -- well, it says here on the 15th of March but I think it was later on in the village of Djilekare by members of the Army of Yugoslavia. After this murder the relative took the bodies to Donja Stubla, that's a village, and the other family members of Smajli Sadiku arrived and they were buried on the spot where they were found. And here you have the official notes made by the policeman on the spot and you can see -- you can trace the course of these activities from the initial information and you can see everything that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you collect information from the ground?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in different ways. The sector methods of work of the police, that's where all the necessary information is gathered and the moment a policeman writes an official note, an official record, it becomes a basis for action. So we invested our best efforts to respond to each and every event, at least by writing up an official record and then we could continue gathering information. The official record was the basis for further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you designate the more able policemen to collect information in various sectors?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already said, we formed teams, we call them operative groups, where the best crime detection policemen were and in the sector as well. Everybody knew in the SUP who was talented to carry out criminal investigations where the police were concerned, who was talented in that respect so that the best policemen worked on crime investigations in the police stations and the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we move on, to whom was this file delivered?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the prosecutor. A criminal report is always submitted to the prosecutor, and that's where the work of the police ends. The moment we hand over either to the civilian or the military prosecutor, the moment we hand over to him or her a criminal report, that's where our work stops. Our work is detection and their work is prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you see to which prosecutor this file was handed over?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor. It was the military prosecutor to whom this file was handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember how many murders were dealt with by the Gnjilane SUP in 1990 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the course of the war, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some statistics. We dealt with 56 murders. We drew up 14 reports for 36 murders, which we submitted to the military prosecutor. We also dealt with 161 cases of arson or fire, and I remember that we took into custody 53 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we clarify the number of murders. You've been recorded in the transcript as saying you dealt with 56 murders but wrote reports for 36. Which is the correct figure or are 36 reported to military prosecutor and 20 civil cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely so. There was a total of 56 murders, 36 were reported to the military prosecutor and 20 to the civilian civil prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's just one more error in the transcript, so I'll ask you. How many persons did you take into custody?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how many days did NATO bomb the area of Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 39 days without interruption, so for 39 days NATO continuously bombed the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these statistics apply to these 70 -- sorry, the period of the NATO bombing, do they? Or do they apply to the whole of 1999 until the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only the period of the NATO bombing, those 72 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to call up in e-court document P1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, we have before us minutes from a meeting with senior police officials in Kosovo and Metohija dated the 4th of April, 1999. Do you remember whether you took part in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, and yes, I did take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the chiefs of SUP reporting about at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said and I'll repeat it now, as for the chiefs of SUP, they reported on the state of safety and security in that area. This is the 4th of April, 1999, that is to say already seven days and more, 10 or 11 days into the war. We reported about that in this initial chaos how the organs of public law and order and the SUP on the whole managed in this situation of chaos, how many people were detained, what kinds of crimes were committed, whether there were any problems in relation to communication, and we saw that there were some and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all chiefs report that they had arrested perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I see that here and I remember that all chiefs had a significant number of arrested persons during the first days of the war. Only the secretariat in Kosovska Mitrovica whose chief was Ljubinko Cvetic did not have a single detained person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when was Ljubinko Cvetic chief of SUP Kosovska Mitrovica, until when did he stay on there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember until the 15th of April, that is to say mid-April that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another ten days or so after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around that, about ten days after this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to call up in e-court 6D614, page 350, paragraph 987.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it to appear on our screens, I'm going to ask you something. During the proofing we showed us Abdylhaqim Shaqiri's statement, he was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2, in paragraph 5, Denic Negovan and Denic Goran are mentioned that they had been seen in military uniforms. Do you remember that that was stated there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please let us look at 987 now. Is there any mention of the Denics here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gnjilane, the 20th of April, 1999, aggravated theft under Article 166. On the 20th of April, 1999, Denic Negovan and Nikolic Aleksandar, both of whom were civilians from the village of Kusce, actually they were from Prilepnica, Nikolic is from Kusce and Denic is from Prilepnica, committed an aggravated theft which is an offence under Article 166 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. The offenders were remanded in custody under Article 196 of the ZKP. The injured party was unknown. Denic Negovan is the person mentioned here, and yesterday we concluded that Goran Denic was also arrested because of arson. They are from the village of Prilepnica, their family is from Prilepnica. I remember these last names like the last names of Pavic from Zegra. So these are the last names that remain in my memory because we had these problems with them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the military?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrested them as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time you established what their status was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this time precisely coincides with the period of time when Prilepnica was empty, when the inhabitants of Prilepnica had left. They left on the 14th of April, the village remained empty, and the theft took place in that village on the 20th of April, 1999, and Denic Negovan and Nikolic Aleksandar were caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you established their status at the time and you established that they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That has to be filed in the criminal report, so when we apprehended them they were treated as civilians, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If they were seen in uniforms of the Army of Yugoslavia, that means that in actual fact that this was an abuse, right; is that what we could infer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that there were such cases. There were such cases, quite a few such cases during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How would you establish their status as civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, he was in civilian clothes and he introduced himself as such. When he was being arrested, he was a civilian, he did not have any uniform on. If he were wearing a uniform, we would know what this is all about, we would report that straight away to the military authorities and then we would establish the identity of the persons concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, thank you. For the time being these were all the questions I had for you. Now other questions will be put to you probably from some other Defence team and then from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gavranic, how are you doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm just going to use up a bit of your time. Mr. Lukic showed you the minutes of the meeting held on the 4th of April, 1999, twice.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up 19 -- P1989, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have it in hard copy, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1989, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you can see, this is the 4th of April, 1999. I would like to draw your attention to the beginning of this document when they say who was present. Is the name Nikola Sainovic there, yes, no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Nikola Sainovic's name is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, please take a look at page 4, page 4, please, and it's the second or third paragraph from the bottom, the big one. You see it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, here it says that the deputy prime minister of the federal government, Nikola Sainovic, joined in. How come?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that at the end of that meeting Mr. Nikola Sainovic walked in. He was the deputy prime minister of the federal government. I think that it was General Obrad Stevanovic who was speaking at that point. He made his excuses and the general gave him the floor, he greeted us briefly, gave us encouragement because Obrad had finished the few sentences he had when he spoke about prosecutions and measures we should take in order to stop this initial chaos. Mr. Sainovic supported that, encouraged us. As far as I can remember, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You wouldn't know why it was that he came there in the first place and what he was doing in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on and then we're going to deal with a different question. Did you attend a meeting that was held at the MUP staff in Pristina on the 7th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court P1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You see the introductory part?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Here we see that at the very beginning of this meeting we see the name of Mr. Nikola Sainovic as one of the attendees.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I can see you attended as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us first of all whether Sainovic stayed on until the end of the meeting, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And do you know -- and do you know what kind of speech he made and what he talked about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to the first meeting, over here Mr. Nikola Sainovic, deputy federal prime minister, came at the beginning of the meeting. He made a political speech and when he finished he left the meeting and we went on working in accordance with the plan that we had, and I've already given my comments with regard to these minute a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On pages 3 and 4 of these minutes, you see that Sainovic gave his comments regarding what -- the statement of the Commander-in-Chief that was released in the Politika daily newspaper?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you aware of that statement before that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received it a day before. I knew about that. I think that on the previous day we received a photocopy of the Politika article, where the head of state spoke about the situation in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at 5D1289. I don't know if you have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You'll see it on your screen in a minute. It is 5D1289. Is that the document that you received?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the second page now. Is that the article or is that not the article?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We don't need the document anymore. So on that day did Sainovic convey to you some kind of directives at that meeting or did he quite simply indicate this text to you, the one that we saw in Politika now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sainovic did not convey any directives to us. Practically he repeated some of the things that we had already read in the newspapers on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So at two meetings, if I understood correctly, these were working meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic showed up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the speaker. There's too much background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I kept hitting this microphone, so I couldn't be heard. You mentioned these two meetings that Nikola Sainovic attended in part. These were some working meetings if I understood you correctly. So now I would like to ask you -- actually, you've already said that. You already said that he made an appropriate political speech on both occasions. We are only interested in two questions, one may seem a bit strange to you but I have to put this question. Was he a member of this MUP staff or did he participate in any way in the work of the MUP or did he influence the work of the MUP in any way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he issue any orders then? Did he give instructions? Was he someone's extended arm? Did he ask you for reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you've been in the MUP for quite a long time, you said that he was deputy federal prime minister. Did the federal government have any authority whatsoever over the republican MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the federal government had no powers over the republican MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one more thing. During the course of 1999 while you were in Kosovo, you from the staff of MUP or down the MUP line, did you see in any way a document ordering something to you and would this be a document stating Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I as the SUP of Gnjilane really never saw a single document that had that kind of heading, Joint Command, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not going to trouble you any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's out of order but I forgot to ask this witness one question. Is it -- if you can allow me so there would be no prejudice to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, Mr. Gavranic. Ljubinko Cvetic testified before this Chamber. He stated that on the 17th of March, 1999, a meeting was held in the MUP staff or MUP headquarters and that Sreten Lukic spoke about volunteers, or rather, the use of volunteers in Kosovo and Metohija. Firstly, do you recall and have you found in your notes that on the 17th of March, 1999, a meeting was actually held in the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there was a meeting in MUP headquarters attended by him in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be on the 17th of February?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the minister speak about volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the minister did speak about volunteers. He said we should be cautious with them in case there was an aggression. This was in the pre-aggression period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second. This all started with you saying, Mr. Lukic, that Sreten Lukic spoke about volunteers. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what Cvetic told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And your question is a different one, is it, did the minister speak about volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because Cvetic said that Mr. Lukic spoke about the volunteers on the meeting of the 17th of March. Now, we first established that it was actually the meeting of the 17th of February, and then I asked about the minister. I'll come to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, which minister are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. All right. Thank you. I thought we had jumped without -- and missed a stage, but okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who spoke about volunteers at that meeting to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, and I remember it well, it was the minister of the interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether at that meeting Sreten Lukic also spoke about volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Sreten Lukic talking about volunteers at that meeting, but I know the minister said that later on we would be receiving instructions in case of an aggression, how we should act in such cases. We never did have volunteers. That's important. The MUP never had volunteers. In the Gnjilane SUP we had not a single volunteer. If people did turn up and report, we sent them on to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to ask additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Gavranic. I have only one question for you. You said more than once that at the collegium held on the 7th of May you reported to that gathering that within the scope of the work of the Gnjilane SUP you submitted 189 criminal reports and arrested 114 persons for crimes committed from the beginning of the aggression up to the 6th of May. My question is only this: Through the system of reporting you have explained to us, did you report this to the ministry in Belgrade through the reporting system in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day. Yes, we did. Through a courier, it was sent in the same way but by means of a courier. The courier would take the post to the office of the SUP in Pristina, to the clerk there, and then it was sent on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gavranic. My name is Djuro Cepic. I appear for the Defence of General Lazarevic this morning. Unfortunately, I'm not as good a footballer as you used to be, but I have a few questions for you in connection with what you said before this honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on our screens 6D852.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document to come up, you explained that the location of Kabas is a place where investigations were carried out when you explained how, but do you remember who reported that crime, that murder, perpetrated by a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find this in the official record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... second page, please. [Interpretation] Could we see page 2, please. [In English] Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that the police went there on receipt of an -- of a report, they went to the village of Kabas where they secured the body of Mustafa Shefqet. And then it goes on to explain how through operative information it was established how the murder had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the person who perpetrated the murder was frightened and pointed their weapon at Shefqet and fired five bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this crime was reported by the military patrol stationed in the village of Kabas on the 5th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the first passage on page 3.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that on the 5th of May at 1620 hours a military patrol -- yes, correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for your reference in Exhibit P955 on page 10 the name of Dragan Stoiljkovic is stated as having committed a crime, the crime of murder, and that he was dealt with by the military prosecutor's office. Can we have in e-court 6D334.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, this morning you gave us a little more information about this exhumation of six freshly dug graves, and we see here that the report was sent to the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, whether you remember whose expert, whose forensic expert or pathologist was present at the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was a military pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your reference regarding the murders in the Gnjilane area, the military judicial organs acted on this, as can be seen in report P955, page 76, and the number of corpses discovered in the entire area is stated; and on page 82 of the same document we see the name of Nebojsa Stojkovic, a reservist from Leskovac who was prosecuted for the crime of murder of several persons, multiple murder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, you spoke about the crime committed by Vlado Zmajevic and others. Am I right in saying that this was in late March and that this group, or rather, these individuals and that Zmajevic and those persons who were with him had just arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I assume you immediately informed the military organs about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we handed over the case file in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see on our screens 5D825.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at item 2, that's a document of the 175th Infantry Brigade of the 31st of March, 1999. If we look at the second sentence in paragraph 2 of item 2, could you read it, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "After demonstrating indiscipline and other criminal activities by certain volunteers, the situation is slowly becoming more stable. Eight volunteers for whom there are reasonable grounds to suspect that they committed a crime in Zegra village have been arrested."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that refer to those volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for your reference, in P955 on page 19 Vlado Zmajevic and others are mentioned. They were prosecuted by the military judicial organs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, my colleague Mr. Lukic asked you about civilians who abused or misused uniforms. I'll show you 5D549 now. Could we look at item 5, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Security. "In the brigade's zone we are also establishing control over those who are not part of the unit strength. Burning and looting by civilians in the population are becoming more frequent. They are dressed in uniforms with different patterns. On the 26th of April, 1999, six persons were found carrying out such activities, two were identified in the act and they were immediately brought before the investigating judge."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the heading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We see that the document was issued by the 175th Brigade on the 27th of April. They were in the Gnjilane area, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether in addition to the examples Mr. Lukic asked you about, were there also other cases where uniforms were misused?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, there were quite a few such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm finding this difficult -- slightly difficult to follow. What -- can you give us an example of -- apart from this one of the abuse or misuse of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, people had uniforms. The civilian defence also had uniforms, but they were not members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Those uniforms -- well, people kept them at home because they'd been issued with them before the war, and then they would put them on, commit a crime, and put it back. So it was very hard to establish who, in fact, perpetrated a crime. I've already said in my previous testimony that later on I heard that Denic was wearing a military uniform. I heard that from the testimony of witness imam which I read, but I didn't know when we arrested him that he had had a uniform. He was a civilian. There were such cases and they were not infrequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why on earth would anyone do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a state of war. There were criminals everywhere. There were criminals even in peacetime who caused us great problems. As soon as they saw that the situation was favourable to them, they would do what they did and they would find the best possible way of doing it without being discovered. They looted abandoned villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that suggests to me that it's okay if you're wearing a uniform, you'll get away with it; otherwise, why on earth would somebody put on a uniform to carry out an act of looting or arson? I'm trying to understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely in order to shift the blame on the Army of Yugoslavia because then it would be difficult to find perpetrators because the army was so big and there were so many soldiers in my area covered by the Gnjilane SUP, there were thousands of soldiers in that area. We in the police -- but that's a different topic. We in police wore bands on sleeves in order to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Lay aside the question of whether members of the KLA might wear uniforms similar to VJ uniforms, but why would a Serb civilian, why on earth would a Serb civilian commit crimes under the cover of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a criminal is a criminal, regardless of what uniform he wears when perpetrating a crime. That's my opinion. I don't know to what extent I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was it easier to move about if one wore a military uniform during the war, Mr. Gavranic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By your leave I would add something. If you had a military uniform, then the army would not check on you. Police would not check as much either. If you had a civilian clothing on you, then both would check on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 4D174, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, we have a document of the Army of Yugoslavia, the security organs, dated the 27th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see item 4 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you see item 4?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: An event which took place on the 18th of April is described therein, the village of Pozaranje. Would you tell me where that village is located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That village is in the territory of the Gnjilane SUP, it's an Albanian village, one of the largest in the territory of the Gnjilane SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this yet another piece of evidence showing that uniformed persons appeared and that they were prosecuted both by the military police -- by the military people and the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apparently they tried to rob somebody and then military police intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They were identified, were they? It says unidentified on what I'm reading, but I've not got the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That only refers to actual members of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no. It says explicitly here that these two men, Djurasevic and Stojkovic were members of the 175th Brigade. As for the village it is stated that this was outside of the area of responsibility of the unit. The unit was not deployed there, so the identity of these persons was not established and this deals with two different events in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, is this a good time for break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination will be lengthy, will it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Better finished after the break, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We break now for half an hour, Mr. Gavranic. Could you again leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before the witness comes in, I would like to introduce a new member of our team, Drazen Djukic, our new legal advisor, who will be helping us in our future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it there is no objection to either of the documents I raised at the beginning of this morning's session? Very well. We shall proceed to make an order accordingly. Mr. Cepic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, just a few more questions. We have in front of us on the screens the same document we dealt with before the break, which is a document of security organ signed by Major Miroslav Panic, 27 of April, 1999. This is the document of the Army of Yugoslavia. Would you please look at item 5.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please read it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 26th of April OB," which I guess is the security organ --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Of the 175th Infantry Brigade brought into detention Dragan Raykovic, son of Petar, and Milivoj Stojiljkovic, son of Djordje, who had set on fire the house of an unidentified Siptar in the village of Radivojce, justifying it by saying that they owed the man 200 German marks. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and carried automatic rifles. They introduced themselves as volunteers from the 175th Infantry Brigade even though they were from the village of Klokot. They will be handed over to the investigating judge with a criminal report on the 28th of April. "That same day, the following civilians from the village of Klokot were brought into detention by the military police for having looted the abandoned Siptar houses in Radivojce village: Nenad Radic, son of Dobrivoj; Goran Stanojevic, son of Trajan; Zoran Radic; Zivojin Aksic. Criminal reports shall be filed against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gavranic, are all these settlements in the territory of the Gnjilane territory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when it comes to what steps military organs took, we have two documents, 5D555 and 5D560. However, this witness does not belong to the Army of Yugoslavia. These two documents deal with the situation and the activities in that area of Gnjilane. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I don't know if this applies to any documents referred to earlier in your cross-examination, but these two are not exhibited. They may be the subject of an application before us at the moment, but until that's resolved they're not part of the process. And simply mentioning documents in the course of your cross-examination will not lead to them being exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to request their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no basis for you requesting their admission, Mr. Cepic. You've just named them, and that's not a basis on which we can deal with such an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, then just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is cross-examination of a witness for another accused. It's not an opportunity for you to present yet another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I just need opportunity for additional bar table, probably we will have -- on Friday we already filed a very, very big motion and we've been waiting for some documents from Belgrade also in relation to previous witnesses from our Defence case. These documents will confirm some allegations and also maybe some other documents, and we will try to file it as soon as it is possible, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know that there are certain issues which you have alerted the Chamber to, but it was made very clear to you that you were being given one final opportunity after your case was closed to put together a motion to present any documents you wished from the bar table, and it's in the course of that process that you've drawn to our attention the difficulty of translation, for example, and some matters of that administrative nature, we will make allowances for. But your case is closed subject to resolving the issues outstanding in relation to exhibits that were outstanding as at the closure of your case. And introducing fresh documents requires the re-opening of your case, and the test for that is a very demanding one which you're not seeking to satisfy at the moment. If, however, this witness has said something that you wish to challenge by referring to a document, then you may do that; and to the extent that he were to accept the accuracy of the document, then it may become part of the record in this case. But that would only apply where you were challenging something that he was saying, or he was a witness through whom you felt something positive could be contributed, and by that I mean from his personal knowledge. You could also try to ask him something from his personal knowledge that might relate to a document and thus make the document part of the case because in cross-examination you are obviously entitled to lead evidence that will also support your case. But it's only something that he would have personal knowledge of that it would be appropriate to do that with. It's not good enough to simply put a document in front of him and ask him to read it and then expect that at this stage that will become part of your case.
