utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 20. I beg your pardon, Your Honour, about 20, around 20. Now, was it 20 or 25 or 17, 18, but 20-odd villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, these persons were issued with weapons by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 I was informed that they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened to the weapons when the war started?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not being armed by the MUP only. I'm not sure, but to the best of my knowledge when the war broke out weapons were collected, these reserve police squads fell apart, and the weapons that were issued to them had to be returned, they had to return it to whoever had issued the weapons to them. They went to the stations where they had been issued with these weapons. They had to return these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of the role, if any, that the MUP staff for Pristina had in controlling and regulating these reserve police entities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the role of the staff in Pristina was in relation to these reserve police squads or entities. I know during this brief period of time how they functioned and what our operative information was regarding the situation in these villages and so on. I really don't know what the role of the staff was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could move on to another area. We have heard testimony from several witnesses, mainly brigade commanders of the VJ, that they liaised with the chiefs of SUPs in order to coordinate anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you speaking for yourself or are you saying that this didn't happen in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking in my own name, in the area of the SUP of Gnjilane I never coordinated any action or did I cooperate along those lines with any brigade commander of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could it be that although you had a problem with terrorists in Gnjilane, Gnjilane wasn't -- the terrorists' activity in Gnjilane wasn't as intensive as in other places?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've already said in 1998 there weren't any terrorist actions. I realized that when hand-over took place, hand-over of duty. There were terrorists but there weren't active terrorists in Gnjilane as opposed to other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P1971. This is a Joint Command order dated the 13th of April, 1999, an order on routing and destroying terrorist forces in the area of Zegovac. Zegovac is pretty close to Gnjilane, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an area that belongs to Gnjilane, Zegovac and Zegovacka Vrbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look in the first paragraph of the order, that is precisely the area it discusses, Zegovac Vrbica in Gnjilane and the village of Plitkovic in Lipljan. And if you go to -- well, I think it's page 1 on your page, if we go to page 2 of the English we will see under 2, tasks of the Pristina Corps as: "Reinforced and assisted by armed non-Albanian population in Kosovo and Metohija shall provide support to MUP forces in routing and destroying the STS," that is the KLA, "in their zone of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said in relation to that meeting that was mentioned several times at the staff in Pristina on the 4th of April, I did refer to this. Our information moved in that direction. You see Lipljan in this area, the Gnjilane-Urosevac-Pristina area is the one that we're talking about, and I do know that there was an anti-terrorist action there in mid-April of the forces of the army and MUP, or rather, PJPs. I know that. However, I've never seen this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what MUP units were involved?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that the manoeuvre company of the Gnjilane SUP went to join the intervention brigade, but I don't know which units took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the -- in reference to the armed non-Albanian population in Kosovo and Metohija, do you know what that reference is about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where is that? I can't see it written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First sentence of item 2. Do you see now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not translated. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Item 2 of page 1 of your document, task of Pristina Corps, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, can you read the first sentence there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes, yes. Oh, no, this is a military document, I've never seen it and I cannot interpret it and I cannot interpret what the military meant by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it says that the operation shall be conducted by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of this Joint Command. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you have heard about the Joint Command today, so you must have heard about it before. When is the first time you heard of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the newspapers started following these trials. In Kosovo, believe me, I never heard of a Joint Command. I never heard of this concept, this Joint Command, or whatever it was. That is a concept that is completely unknown to me. Later on a lot was said about that in the press and at trials, but I've never seen a single document to be able to say, Ah, yes, I have seen this document where it says Joint Command, never, truly, least of all do I know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this document here seems to be referring to a fairly large operation. How many of your men were involved in this operation in mid-April?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, one company. It is that PJP company, this manoeuvre company, it went out on this mission. How many people took part in this area, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When these units -- I understand that you don't know because I think I understand what you're saying. When your unit joined with other MUP units in these operations, who commanded them? Who commanded the MUP units in these operations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit did not join these units in that operation. There is the usual procedure that is followed, the company commander reports to the commander of the brigade, and he goes there and receives an assignment. So it's not that it is attached to it. It goes to be within its brigade when called up, as invited by the brigade commander. It is not joint from the SUP. It always goes to the headquarters to its own brigade, and from there they go into certain actions, and chiefs of SUP don't know anything about these actions. I already told you about that, that I knew about this action, because I provided for everything that I told you about in terms of the consequences of this action, but how many people took part, how many members of the PJP, for example, how many companies were involved and how many soldiers, for instance, no, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You don't know. My last question on this topic, and if you don't know, you don't know. When more than one detachment or units of PJP are involved in large operations, who in the MUP commands or coordinates these large MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of the MUP secretariats certainly don't know that. I never had more than this one manoeuvre company that went out to its own brigade. Now, who commanded, I just told you -- I told you that I just know who the commander of the brigade was, Brakovic, I found out about that; however, who commands the other brigades, I only saw some people when they attended meetings and when I attended these meetings. I mean, chiefs of SUP do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you will agree with me, even if you might not know about the large operation, but if there are small operations within your own SUP you would have to send the combat plans to the ministry staff for approval?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I requested only if I needed that, but I didn't have such cases, but there were some OPGs that were used for searches, then I would ask for approval to use members of the PJP. I could not involve them apart from regular tasks for anything else. Am I clear on that? So I would receive approval to have them engaged in risky actions when we're talking about the SUP of Gnjilane. I did not have any anti-terrorist actions in the area of the SUP of Gnjilane where I would engage members of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you receive approval from the ministry staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approval for what? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For action by the units within your SUP.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm telling you that I did not have such actions, but I would ask for approval. Had we planned on that if we had a smaller group that we needed to eliminate, I've already told you that the company commander would have to report to his commander, to his commander, and then I would get approval for engaging them on this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just look at one last document in this area, Mr. Gavranic, and move on. Could you look at P1993, the MUP staff minutes of the 11th of May. Sorry, they are not MUP staff minutes, but it is a record of a meeting held at the MUP staff on the 11th of May. And --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th -- oh, yes, yes, I see that now. I thought it was my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Page 13 of the English and I'm afraid I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are you looking for? Maybe I can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 13 of the English where Lieutenant-General Stevanovic addressed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It could be page 6 in B/C/S. Is it under number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I think that the witness wasn't present on this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read, sir, from the 7th of May or immediately after what Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic said when he's introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, this is 11th of May I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document is the 11th of May. I would like him to read where the text says the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part would you like? I have the minutes dated the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? Somebody put some kind of a sticker here if you look at the Serbian original on the right-hand side, and Mr. Stamp would like him to read something that is actually printed below this sticker. On the sticker there's a handwritten note saying: "Less action," you see it says in Serbian less action, "manje akcija," so he can't read what it is that you want him to read from that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the witness has documents in front of him which he has brought. Perhaps he has a copy that is not obliterated blocked. I would like him to read from what he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He has my copy, my copy has the same sticker on it. If you provide him with a copy that does not, then he might have without the sticker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's ask a question, Mr. Stamp, and then we'll see where we go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that we have one in e-court without the sticker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you just ask a question. This is taking forever. It must be something very significant, I appreciate, but let's just ask a question. That's what you're here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand the witness has one without a sticker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I would like to ask would be to some degree dependent on what the document reads. Do you have a copy of the minutes for the 11th of May meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He appears to be on the page that you're looking for. What is it you want read? Paragraph 1 or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The section where Lieutenant-General Stevanovic addresses the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have we got that in -- yes, we've got that in English on the page. So you want him to read on the 7th of May, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that -- of those minutes of the 11th of May without the sticker which obliterates part of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the 11th of May at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I've never attended a meeting, not on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have the minutes for the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the minutes of the 7th of May. Just tell me what it is that I'm supposed to read out. I have the minutes from the meeting held at the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is before the witness is P1993. Mr. Stamp, ask your question, please. Either that or we'll move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see on the document in front of you, Witness, that General Stevanovic is ordering that every SUP and PJP will establish a priority list of anti-terrorist action with details of plans which is to be approved by the staff, and perhaps I'm belabouring the point, but this is another document indicating that the SUPs were involved in planning anti-terrorist action and the staff in Pristina would have to approve their plans. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I explained how the SUPs participated because I did not have such things, but I have explained how the SUPs acted when members of the PJP were supposed to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, you have a document there which at the top right-hand corner had the number K0497277. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's got something stuck on it obliterating part of the writing so you can't read it, but then there is paragraph 1. Now, would you read the third line, from the third line of paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood. "Now we need to organize smaller-scale actions or plan dotted, closely linked actions in more minor positions (places). Every SUP and every PJP detachment will establish a priority list of anti-terrorist actions with detailed plans which will be approved by the staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in English that sounds pretty clear and straightforward that the PJP detachments and the SUPs have to establish a priority list of anti-terrorist actions. Do you agree that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had I had detachments in my territory, I would have known what this means, but I didn't have any detachments in the Gnjilane SUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, please answer my question. Do you agree that that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you also agree that these actions have to have detailed plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that these have to be approved by the staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not by the staff. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not what the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The plans are approved -- it says here the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That's all I want to know. Now, are you saying -- are you saying that from your experience in Kosovo that that is nonsense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no personal experience. I did not have any detachments. I could simply give you my own opinion, whatever it's worth. As for my experience, I simply don't have it because we didn't have detachments, we didn't plan any actions, and I had no experience regarding these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on. Do you know of a group called the Skorpions being in Gnjilane, a group -- a paramilitary group known as the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not area of them, and I don't think that there ever existed any paramilitary group in Gnjilane called Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which case we'll move on again. You spoke in your evidence about the imam or the priest I think you called him from Prilepnica. Is that Abdylhaqim Shaqiri that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Prilepnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that the persons who came to the village and forced them out or told them that they had to leave on the 13th of April including -- included Binacka Morava -- sorry, included a lawyer from Binacka Morava called Djilas Mladenovic. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lawyer from Binacka Morava, no, I'm not aware -- he mentioned I think Ljuba Palamarovic, not Mladenovic, and Ljuba Palamarovic is a lawyer all right. I heard that he -- that such a person exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Correct. He said that this Ljuba Palamarovic, whatever his profession was, was one of the persons who chased them out of the village. Did you know that in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I learned that from the statement and I've told you that we couldn't establish who it was who had given them such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you ever told that one of the persons there was also Djilas Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw all that in the statement. I never heard about that, I didn't know -- we didn't establish who it was to whom they belonged. No, we never learned of that. All of the consultations we conducted then on the 6th when they returned, indicated that none of the officers in the army whom I knew had any idea who could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you also said in respect to the moving out -- these people moving out, you said in your evidence that the Serbs also moved out because they feared revenge. What do you mean by that when you said they feared revenge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that when I mentioned Zegra. When first murders took place in Zegra in late March, since the population was mixed there and those who were killed were Albanians, Zegra, which is a village with mixed population, what happened there was that Serbs came to the centre of Gnjilane, several hundred of Serbs came there, because they feared revenge. They took their women and children out of the village because they feared that the Albanians would take revenge. And in early April they went back, they convinced them to go back to Zegra.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Shaqiri said that when he returned to his village at the end of June, that's Prilepnica, he found that it had been completely burned. Do you know that, that the village had been completely burned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Prilepnica was completely burned. Individual houses were and, yes, the property was looted and I've already told you that we arrested some people who were caught in the act.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many villages in your SUP region had houses burnt down?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know how many fires resulted in prosecutions, but as for houses, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There was also a mosque at the Vlastica area in Gnjilane. Do you know that mosque?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the village of Vlastica there was a mosque and I also know that it was burned down, that it burned down. I also know that upon receiving a report from an Albanian we organized some large machinery to go to the ruins because he claimed that his parents were under the ruins and we managed to get there some excavators and other construction machinery and saw that what he said was quite right, his parents were under the wreckage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We conducted an on-site investigation and we filed a criminal report, a criminal complaint, against unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was the -- I take it that you don't know anything or very much about the actions of your PJP units once they were in the field. Could you tell us who was the commander of the PJP, your PJP unit or company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rizanovic Dragan was the company commander. He was also deputy commander of the 124th Brigade, Zarko Brakovic. When he became deputy, then Vasic Goran became company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further for this witness, Your Honours. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranic, you were asked just a short time ago about your reference to Serb fear of revenge when you were dealing with events in late March, revenge from whom?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the KLA. We had information in that area, and that is the area leading towards the Macedonian border, that it was the KLA, the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But revenge for what then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning those first murders in Zegra. Three Albanians were killed, and then the Serbs fearing revenge set out towards Gnjilane. They were afraid to spend that night in Zegra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you've left the impression towards the end of your evidence there that a number of villages around your area may have been burned and looted when the Albanians were not there. Is that a fair impression for us to form?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you've left me also with the impression that the destruction of the Vlastica mosque was just a wanton act of damage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It burnt down. How that happened, we don't know, but it was burned down to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not a criticism, but in -- at the beginning of your evidence when you were telling us about yourself there was no indication that you had any formal training in police work. Did you have formal training for service in the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How then did you come to be the chief of the SUP in Serbia, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came there from the position of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. Up until that time, chief of SUPs were part of municipal government, municipal authorities. They were members of municipal government up until that time. Later on that was changed in 1992. So somebody believed that I was familiar with these matters and new territorial SUPs had been established, and since I was from the area they believed that I could help significantly with the organization. I thought that it would be of short duration; however, that wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was 1992, in fact, that you became chief of the SUP; is that right, just before things --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before the rules changed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you at that time a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was a member of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judging by Mr. Cepic's introduction to you, you may be well-known as a sporting star of the past. The football team that you played for, how was it financed? Was it financed from a political background or an army background or a police background?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The football club I played for Proleter Zrenjanin was part of the town of Zrenjanin, it was financed by the Municipal Assembly of the town of Zrenjanin. It did not belong to any political party or any institution, be it military or police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know why you were selected to go to Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the total number of policemen in Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was some 450 policemen in Gnjilane, about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour. It will be a shame not to ask this witness at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavranic, you spoke about arrests of dangerous persons or terrorists and occasional use of OPGs, operational pursuit groups. You said that occasionally you would report to the staff. First of all, did you use these people as members of your SUP or as members of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used those people as members of my SUP because I knew who was trained for those kinds of assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These reports, did you send them before actions, in the course of actions, or after actions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you for testifying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you still play football?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I still do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For recreational purposes, and I am involved with children. I have a football school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Watching you come in and out of the court, I envy your fitness. That completes your evidence, Mr. Gavranic. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, P1993, I think you ought to provide us with a copy without a sticker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was hoping -- I thought that the witness had a copy without a sticker. But as it turns out, a copy without a sticker was located and I could now seek your leave to put that copy with the appropriate translation into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another issue in respect to the exhibits, and this is in respect to Exhibit 6D614, a large volume of excerpts of reports that was used for the first time with this witness. Generally the practice has been that where a document is shown to a witness in the course of his examination and the witness can speak meaningfully about and it's relevant in a forensic sense, the document is marked as admitted in e-court. And there's nothing wrong with that practice in a general sense. However, in this particular sense what we have here is a long document numbering almost 800 pages I think in B/C/S. And the witness was able to speak only in respect to certain extracts from the document. And in those circumstances I'd respectfully ask that even if the document itself is received in evidence for practical purposes, the parts of the document that are treated as evidence be only those which the witness could personally speak on and not the entire 700 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll bring the witness who composed this document -- actually, this document serves us not to translate thousands of pages based on which this compilation is made and we'll have the witness who worked on composing of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's clear that so far only the parts spoken to by the witness are admitted. He had personal knowledge of the individual events that were highlighted in your examination, and we'll treat those as -- those extracts as admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll deal with the rest as and when the issue arises. Does that clarify it, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the next witness is the one to be led by Mr. Zorko, is that correct? Mr. Zorko, who is that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Zivko Lekoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lekoski. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document that will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be -- you will now be examined by Mr. Zorko on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Zorko -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First me. Sorry. We asked for the Macedonian interpreter for this witness, but we were late. So the gentleman will be listening to Serbian translation and will be answering in Serbian, but of course it's not his mother tongue. So please have some patience with this witness. We were late. We didn't know that we have to apply two weeks in advance. We applied I think just a week in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Interpretation is an art that is in very limited supply, particularly for certain languages, and arrangements do have to be made well in advance of the attendance of witnesses who require these special arrangements. And because there is a case which requires constant Macedonian interpretation in this court, then you have to be alert to the need to apply earlier for additional facility for Macedonian in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Fila could translate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall do as you request, Mr. Lukic, and exercise restraint and hope to make reasonable progress. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lekoski.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: My name is Boris Zorko, I'm a lawyer in the Lukic Defence team, and we were just explained here that we will not have the assistance of interpreters here, so I would kindly ask you to speak slowly so that everything can be properly recorded. For the sake of the record, would you please give us your name, last name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I'm Zivko Lekoski, I was born on the 6th of August, 1954, in Gostivar, the Republic of Macedonia. I apologise if I make any mistakes in terms and could I kindly ask the Defence to correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No one needs to apologise for language difficulties in this court. We understand your position entirely, Mr. Lekoski, and we are doing our best to conduct the proceedings in a way that will avoid any misunderstanding. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is your ethnic background? I will repeat my question. Can you tell us about your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I'm a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell us something briefly about your education, about your employment, if any, and what is your current position.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I completed secondary school, I worked in several companies in Gostivar. My last employment was as manager of the Toza Markovic company from Kikinda in the FRY, this was a representative office in Skoplje and I was its manager. I am currently unemployed. Sometimes I get work in various companies as an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, do you speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: As I completed primary school in an Albanian village and I live in Gostivar, where 67 per cent of the population is Albanian, they are in the majority, I understand a word here and there but I can understand more than I can speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in the course of 1999, did you travel to Serbia or the FRY and how often if you did?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: In the course of 1999 I travelled more than once. I can't recall precisely, but I am sure that I travelled to Serbia four or five times while the air-strikes were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court Exhibit 6D1496.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognise the document, it's my old passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I do apologise, but on page 2, do the details you can read here correspond to the details in your old passport?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document remain on e-court and could we look at page 6 of the document, which is page 11 of the passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski -- I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could the witness be shown the image so that he can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Could you look at the stamp? There should be a stamp which says Donje Blace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 6 of e-court if it could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have the correct page on e-court. Mr. Lekoski, on this page of your passport you can see a stamp marked Donje Blace?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And the date on this stamp is the 27th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Is it correct that you crossed the border on that date, the border with the FRY, and entered Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to the Republic of Serbia from the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you tell us what was the reason why several days after the start of air-strikes you travelled to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I have a sister in Serbia who lives in Blace, it's a town close to Krusevac, and I went to visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. For the sake of precision, Donje Blace is the border crossing on the Macedonian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness also be shown page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And I'll ask you whether you passed through the border crossing of Djeneral Jankovic on the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell us how you crossed the border on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I came to the border crossing, Donje Blace, in the Republic of Macedonia by taxi, and then I crossed the border on foot, as far as the border crossing called Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When crossing the border you are now talking about, on the 27th of March, 1999, did you observe civilians at the border crossing; and if so, on what side of the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: When I arrived by taxi at the Donje Blace border crossing of the Republic of Macedonia, I noticed about a dozen civilians crossing the border at that point in time. They were mostly elderly people and there were a few women with children in their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there men in this group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: There were men, yes, but mostly elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you talk about these civilians, were you able to observe any signs of mistreatment, such as torn clothing, bruises, or anything else that might indicate mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything like that. What I did notice was that they looked frightened, a little bit frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You mentioned civilians. Apart from the civilians, was there anybody else at the border crossing; and if so, can you tell us who?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, there was a team of journalists, there was a camera in the middle of the road bearing the words CNN and there were two persons standing next to the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you describe the persons standing next to the camera?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: The man standing right next to the camera was tall. In my assessment, he was about 180 centimetres tall. He was wearing a dark jacket. The other one was a little shorter than the first one, swarthy, dark, and he was holding a microphone in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did anything attract your attention; and if so, can you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Well, yes. What attracted my attention was the fact that a camera which was standing on a tripod of sorts was some 15 metres or so away from the border crossing in an area where usually cars cross the border. And the camera was filming the civilians who were moving towards it. At that point in time, when the civilians got close to the camera, the man holding a microphone in his hand approached the people and he told them in the Albanian language "Pseiku," which in translation would mean: Why are you fleeing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did the civilians reply and what did they do next?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: When they heard this they started waving their arms about, looking up at the sky, and they said NATO bombs and similar things. And when the man holding the microphone heard what they were saying, he said to them: "Jo NATO jo bomb," which would mean in translation, don't mention bombs, don't mention NATO, but he said to them in Albanian that they should say "vrau policia Serbe," which would mean they had been beaten by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Did anything else happen after that that you can describe?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: Well, when they heard this, a woman with a child in her arms who was right in front of the camera probably not able to understand why they were asking her this, she moved on and passed by the camera. And the man holding the microphone in his hand grabbed hold of her hands and started dragging her back. He said to her in Albanian: "Shko prapa," which in translation would mean: Come back. But this woman, again not understanding why they were asking her this, wrenched herself out of his grip and the man with a microphone in his hand hit her, he slapped her, in fact. She started crying, and as a response to the mother's tears the child began to cry too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. What was the person next to the camera doing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: When the woman started crying, the person standing next to the camera took the camera off the tripod and came closer to this woman in order to film her crying. And through her tears the man with a microphone told her to say what he had told her to say and she in tears said "Me vrau policia Serbe," which would mean I was beaten by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: What did you do after this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI
utterances.text: I didn't do anything. I crossed the border, and as I had agreed with a friend of mine from Pristina, he was waiting for me at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing in the FRY and he gave me a lift and took me to see my sister in Blace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a good time to interrupt if it's convenient for you. Mr. Lekoski, regrettably we have to bring our proceedings for the day to an end at this stage. That means that tomorrow you will require to return here to complete your evidence. That will again be in this courtroom, but tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Meanwhile, between now and then it is a strict rule that you have no communication with anyone about the evidence in this case, and by anyone I mean anyone at all. You can speak about any other subject, but you cannot communicate with anyone about evidence in this case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of February, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24
